findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous denials can deny renderer requests
findings.body: The denial cache key is built from checkReq.UserUID but not checkReq.IdentityType. Both `anonymous:0` and `render:0` parse to the same userUID `0` in validateSubject, so a denied anonymous Check for a dashboard/folder creates the same permDenialCache key that a later renderer Check for the same namespace/action/name/folder will hit. The renderer path would normally return allowed for `dashboards:read` via getRendererPermissions, but the cached denial is returned first. An attacker who can cause repeated anonymous denied checks can keep this entry warm and deny rendering for that resource.

findings.title: Denial cache key concatenation permits collisions between different resource tuples
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent with underscore separators without escaping or length delimiting. These values are not prevented from containing underscores, and an empty parent adds a trailing separator. For example, name=`a_b`, parent=`` produces the same key as name=`a`, parent=`b` for the same user/action. A cached denial for one dashboard/folder can therefore incorrectly deny another resource. Use length-prefixed or hashed components to make the tuple unambiguous.

findings.title: Denial cache test does not prove denial cache is being used
findings.body: The test `Should deny on explicit cache deny entry` sets the permission cache to `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}` and leaves fakeStore permissions empty. If the denial cache lookup were removed or its key did not match, the cached false permission and empty DB result would still produce `Allowed: false`, so the test passes without exercising the denial cache. It should set the cached permission to `true` or provide a DB permission that would allow the request, so the assertion fails if the denial cache is not consulted.
